what_its_for: This medicine is a combination birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (norgestimate) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (the release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the lining of the uterus. Some brands are also approved to treat moderate acne in women who want birth control at the same time.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day, at the same time each day. Consistency is very important — taking it at the same time helps it work best and reduces side effects like nausea. You may take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or at bedtime. Swallow the pill whole with water. Follow the pill pack in order — do not skip pills or take them out of order. After finishing one pack, start the next pack the very next day (or as directed on your pack). The inactive (reminder) pills at the end of the pack do not contain hormones — they help you stay in the habit of taking a pill every day.
dosing: Take one active (hormone) pill daily for 21 days, then take the inactive reminder pills (if included) for 7 days, then start a new pack. Some packs are 28-day packs with 7 inactive pills; others may vary slightly. Your doctor will choose the specific strength and type for you. Do not take more than one pill per day. If you are starting for the first time, your doctor may advise you to start on the first day of your period or on the first Sunday after your period begins. Use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days if you are starting mid-cycle.
missed_dose: Try your best not to miss a pill. If you miss ONE active pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking two pills in one day. Then continue taking one pill per day as usual. No backup birth control is needed. If you miss TWO active pills in a row in weeks 1 or 2: Take two pills on the day you remember and two pills the next day. Then take one pill per day for the rest of the pack. Use a backup method (like condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss TWO active pills in a row in week 3, or if you miss THREE or more active pills in a row: Talk to your pharmacist or doctor right away. You may need to use backup birth control or restart your pack. If you miss any inactive (reminder) pills, simply throw away the missed ones and continue with the pack as scheduled. If you are unsure what to do, use a backup birth control method and call your healthcare provider.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep pills away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture — do not store in the bathroom. Keep the pill pack in its original packaging. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills past the expiration date printed on the package. If you no longer need the medication, ask your pharmacist about the best way to safely dispose of unused pills.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking, especially if you are 35 years of age or older. Smoking while taking birth control pills significantly increases the risk of serious heart problems, blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid taking this medicine if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice in large amounts, as it may affect how the medication works. Be cautious with herbal supplements like St. John's Wort, which can make your birth control less effective. Avoid missing pills, as this greatly reduces protection against pregnancy. Tell all your doctors and pharmacists about every medicine you take, because some antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medications, and HIV drugs can make birth control pills less effective. Avoid prolonged bed rest or long periods of inactivity (like long flights) without talking to your doctor, as birth control pills can increase the risk of blood clots.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you have any of these warning signs — sometimes remembered as ACHES: Abdominal pain (severe stomach pain), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headaches (severe or sudden), Eye problems (blurred vision, loss of vision), or Severe leg pain or swelling. Also call your doctor if you experience: yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), a new lump in your breast, signs of depression or significant mood changes, unusually heavy or prolonged vaginal bleeding, no period for two months in a row (you may be pregnant), severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling, difficulty breathing), or high blood pressure. Contact your provider before stopping the pill if you are planning surgery, as you may need to stop the pill several weeks before a procedure.
when_it_works: If you start taking the pill on the first day of your period, you are protected against pregnancy right away. If you start on any other day, use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days. Birth control pills are about 99% effective when taken correctly every day. With typical use (occasional missed pills), they are about 91% effective. For acne improvement, it may take 6 to 8 weeks of consistent use before you notice a significant difference in your skin.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking this pill, stop taking it and contact your doctor. Breastfeeding: This medication is generally not recommended for women who are breastfeeding, especially in the first few weeks after delivery, because the estrogen can reduce milk supply. Talk to your doctor about progestin-only options if you are nursing. Teenagers: This medication is safe and effective for teens who have already started their menstrual periods. Older adults (over 35): Women over 35 who smoke should not use this medication due to a high risk of blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Women over 35 who do not smoke may use it but should discuss risks with their doctor. Women approaching menopause should talk to their doctor about whether this is still appropriate. Liver problems: Do not use this medication if you have serious liver disease. Migraines with aura: Tell your doctor if you have migraines with aura (visual disturbances before the headache), as this combination pill may not be safe for you.
